implementation_notes: The de-facto Go breaker is gobreaker: gobreaker.NewCircuitBreaker[T](Settings{...}) owns the state machine and Execute(func() (T, error)) is the guarded call. Settings carries ReadyToTrip (the trip predicate over Counts), Timeout (cooldown), MaxRequests (half-open trials), Interval and BucketPeriod (fixed versus rolling window), IsSuccessful and IsExcluded (failure classification) and OnStateChange (observability), so the Go-specific decisions are the error-first signature and the fact that Execute re-panics a panic after counting it as a failure. The standard library has no breaker, so this library (or the stdlib-only variant) is the realization; keep one instance per dependency, because Counts are per instance and a breaker built per request never accumulates enough failures to trip.
pitfalls: Executing a request that blocks forever still occupies the caller: the breaker decides admission only, so pass a context with a timeout to the dependency call.
Counts live in the instance, so a breaker created per request never accumulates failures while one shared across dependencies merges failure domains.
A panic inside Execute is counted as a failure and then re-panicked; recovering it elsewhere without re-arming the call path hides it from the metrics.
ReadyToTrip is only consulted on failures in the closed state and receives a copy of Counts, so trip on a ratio with a minimum Requests floor or a cold breaker trips on its first errors.

variants.name: Hand-rolled breaker with sync/atomic and time.Now (stdlib only)
variants.idiom_name: atomic.Int32 state + atomic.Int64 counters + atomic trip instant
variants.implementation_notes: Without any dependency the breaker is a small struct of stdlib Go: an atomic.Int32 state, atomic.Int64 failure and total counters (the typed atomics added in Go 1.19), and an atomic.Int64 holding the trip time; admission is one load plus, in the open state, a compare-and-swap into half-open, and counting happens after the call returns. time.Now() is the monotonic source in Go - it carries the monotonic reading that the runtime uses for timers - so a cooldown expressed with time.Since survives wall-clock adjustments. Choose this over gobreaker when the dependency budget is zero, when the trip rule is unusual, or when the breaker is a field of an existing struct; choose gobreaker when you want the rolling window, exclusion and state-change callbacks for free.
pitfalls: Mixing clocks (storing wall-clock seconds while comparing against time.Since) breaks the cooldown whenever the clock is adjusted; keep the monotonic reading.
Counters updated as plain int fields across goroutines are a data race that go test -race catches and production tolerates silently.
A ratio computed from counters that are never reset grows stale in the closed state, so add a window or a periodic reset.
The half-open transition needs its own trial counter: a bare CAS either admits every caller or rejects all of them once the state flips.
